The models were used to generate energy and mass balances, which were used as the basis for generating the capital and operating cost estimates. Performance and process limits were based upon published reports, information obtained from vendors and users of the technology, performance data from design/build projects, and best engineering judgment. Most capital and operating costs were estimated by scaling costs available from prior studies using NETL QGESS methodology. Select capital and consumable costs were provided by Black & Veatch (B&V). All costs are in January-2023 dollars. A levelized cost of ammonia (LCOA) was calculated for each case and is used as the key economic metric for the study. 2.1 SYSTEM BOUNDARY The system boundary for the TEA was defined according to the dotted lines shown in Exhibit 2-2. The scope starts at the plant gate where natural gas enters and goes through feed pre- processing and reforming steps. Air is used as an oxidant for the system and provides the nitrogen for ammonia production. Next, the produced syngas goes through a series of cleanup steps, in which CO is removed and either emitted or captured. Finally, the mixture of hydrogen 2 and nitrogen are converted to ammonia. For capture cases, the cost estimate includes CO 2 transport and storage (T&S) costs; however, it is not modeled as part of the study. Ammonia T&S was not considered within the scope of the TEA and, therefore, not modeled nor costed. 16 COMPARISON OF COMMERCIAL, STATE-OF-THE-ART, FOSSIL-BASED AMMONIA PRODUCTION Exhibit 2-2. Plant boundary for the TEA 2.2 SITE CHARACTERISTICS The plant site was selected to be a generic location in the U.S. Midwest to be consistent with the NETL H Baseline study (Lewis, et al., 2022). This selection is also consistent with the 2 location of 11 currently operating ammonia plants in the United States (Fernandez, 2024). Locating the plant in the Midwest enables ammonia off-take by the agriculture industry for use as fertilizer. For the capture cases, a nearby option is available for CO storage in the Illinois 2 Basin. The plant site is assumed to have characteristics and ambient conditions as presented in Exhibit 2-3 and Exhibit 2-4, consistent with the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) ambient conditions for a generic U.S. Midwest plant location, as defined in the “Process Modeling Design Parameters” QGESS document (NETL, 2025d).
